resources.string: A handwriting keyboard where every letter is a single stroke, inspired by the input method of 1990s PDAs (English and Japanese)

1. Tap “Enable keyboard” and turn on Uni-Stroke IME
2. Tap “Switch keyboard” and select it as your input method
3. Tap the text box below to open the writing area

The left two-thirds of the writing area is the letter zone and the right third is the number zone. A stroke is only matched against the zone it was written in, so always write digits on the right.

There is no fixed bar across the top. A column of five buttons (64dp wide, about 47dp each) runs down the left edge of the writing area.

 ⌫ word … Deletes the word before the cursor, or the word you are still writing. Hold it to keep deleting one word at a time
 ◀ ▶ … Move the cursor left and right. Hold to repeat. A word in progress is committed first
 All … Tap to select everything in the field and tap again to delete it. Hold it to select only the word you just picked from the suggestion bar; tap again to delete just that word, or simply write over it.
 If you have moved the cursor or written anything since, holding selects everything instead. This button only ever deletes a selection it made itself, never one you made in the app
 ? … Tap to show or hide the stroke chart. Hold to open Settings

Hold a finger still in the writing zone to start voice input (only while “Hold for voice input” is shown there). It commits by itself when you stop talking, so there is nothing to press at the end (✕ cancels). The hold is longer than a tap, so tapping for punctuation works as before.

Say just “enter”, “delete” or “undo” and it is carried out as a command instead of being typed. With continuous voice input on, one hold keeps listening until you say “stop listening”. The full list of phrases is in Settings. By default only on-device speech recognition is used.

Shift (⇧ / ⇧⇧) and symbol shift (• = Punctuation / ＼ = Extended) are shown in a small indicator at the top right of the writing area. The letters themselves appear underlined in the text field as you write, so they are not echoed on the pad.

On an unfolded foldable or a tablet (smallest width 600dp or more) the keyboard floats: the panel keeps its phone width (420dp), sits at the bottom on your writing-hand side, and everything outside it is fully transparent.

The app behind stays full-screen, and taps and scrolls on the transparent area go straight through to it. The suggestion bar matches the panel width, so the free side always shows the app.

The suggestion bar is stacked above the writing area. When suggestions appear the keyboard simply grows upward; the writing zone and the buttons never shrink. With no suggestions the bar folds away.

Tap [?] at the bottom of the button column to lay the stroke chart over the writing area. Tap [?] again to close it. Writing is ignored while the chart is open, to avoid accidental input.\n\nThe chart is drawn from the very templates used for recognition, so it always matches what the recogniser expects (K, X and + are drawn with a slightly larger loop for legibility; the direction of the loop is identical). ● marks where a stroke starts and the arrow shows where it ends. The sections are letters, common commands, digits, Punctuation and Extended; drag to scroll.

abc / Abc / ABC
 The shift stroke (a vertical line from bottom to top) cycles: once = next letter is a capital, twice = Caps Lock, three times = off. The indicator at the top right shows ⇧ or ⇧⇧.

Automatic capitals
 At the start of a sentence ⇧ lights up by itself, in text fields that ask for it (messages, notes and so on; not usernames or email addresses). Write the shift stroke once to cancel it and start in lower case. This can be turned off in Settings.

Words
 The letters you write are held as an underlined word. A space stroke, a punctuation mark or Return commits it exactly as written; nothing is ever auto-corrected. While the word is underlined the suggestion bar offers completions (see “Word suggestions”).
 Digits end the current word and are entered as they are.

 In password, email, URL and number fields, and in fields where the app has asked for no suggestions, each letter is entered directly and no suggestions are shown.
Kana-kanji conversion is part of the Japanese version. Set the language to 日本語 in Settings to use it.

While you write a word, the suggestion bar shows up to 10 words that begin with it. Tap one to enter the whole word followed by a space.

Suggestions come from two places, both on the device:
 1. Words you have used … remembered with how often and how recently you used them (up to 1,000). A word that is not in the dictionary, such as a name, is offered once you have used it twice
 2. The built-in dictionary … about 77,000 English words ranked by how common they are, so suggestions work from the first word

Apostrophes are optional: write “dont” for don't or “im” for I'm. Capitals follow what you wrote: start with a capital and the suggestions are capitalised, write in Caps Lock and they are all capitals.

After you pick a suggestion:
 . , ! ? : ; … are tucked against the word and followed by a space (“word. ”)
 A space stroke … is not doubled
 A backspace stroke … puts back what you had written, so a wrong pick costs one stroke

Nothing you write is sent anywhere. Suggestions are not shown in password, email, URL or number fields, and words are not remembered in incognito tabs.

This keyboard does not send what you type anywhere. Conversion and prediction run entirely on the device, from your typing history and the built-in dictionary.

Only if you turn on “Online conversion” are readings sent out, to improve kana-kanji conversion.

Sent when it is on
 • Only the hiragana reading you want converted
 • The destination is Google's conversion service

Never sent, even when it is on
 • The contents of password, email and URL fields
 • The contents of fields where the app has refused learning, such as incognito tabs
 • The text you commit, your contacts, your location or any device identifier

Separately, when you open this app's screens it asks GitHub whether an update is available. Only the question “what is the latest version?” is sent, never anything you typed (the server sees your IP address). You can turn this off in Settings.

You can change this at any time in Settings.

While this is off, nothing you type is sent anywhere (conversion and prediction use only your history and the built-in dictionary).

When it is on, only the hiragana reading you want converted is sent to Google's conversion service, which improves kana-kanji conversion.

Even when it is on, nothing is sent from password, email or URL fields, or from fields where learning is refused, such as incognito tabs.
On — send readings for better conversion

This keyboard comes with a core dictionary of about 80,000 words, so Japanese works offline straight away.

Adding the extended dictionary (about 220,000 words / about 6.7 MB) improves the conversion of names and technical terms.

This only downloads one dictionary file. Nothing you type is sent (it is unrelated to “Online conversion”).

Wi-Fi is recommended. You can also install it later from Settings.

The core dictionary (about 80,000 words) is built in, so conversion works offline without the extended dictionary. The extended dictionary (about 220,000 words) is better at names and technical terms.\n\nOnly the dictionary file is downloaded; nothing you type is sent. The file\'s SHA-256 hash is checked and it is opened as a dictionary before it replaces the current one. A damaged file is discarded and the current dictionary keeps working.
Now: core dictionary (about 80,000 words, built in)
Now: core dictionary (about 80,000 words, built in)\nExtended dictionary v%1$d is installed and becomes active with Premium

Turning this on does not cause periodic network use. It only checks whether a newer extended dictionary is out when you open the app\'s screens and at least 7 days have passed since the last check. This is separate from app updates.

“Automatic” uses online conversion only while Online conversion is on, and switches to the on-device engine by itself when you are offline or the request fails or times out.

“On-device only” never uses the network for conversion, even when Online conversion is on.

While Online conversion is off, only the on-device engine runs whichever you choose. Candidates made by the on-device engine are marked “on-device” at the right end of the candidate bar.

A dictionary and a kana-kanji conversion engine are built in for when the network is unavailable.

The engine builds a lattice from the dictionary and picks the most likely segmentation and spelling with the Viterbi algorithm. Word costs and connection costs both come from Mozc's open data.

The dictionary file is memory-mapped as it is, so start-up stays fast and almost no memory is used.

When you open this app's screens it asks GitHub whether a newer version is out (at most once a day).

Only the question “what is the latest version?” is sent; nothing you typed is included. As with any connection, the server sees your IP address.

This never happens while you are typing. If you turn it off, the check only runs when you press “Check now” below.
Could not check for updates (network error)
The download could not be found
Not enough free space to save the download
To install the update, this device has to allow Uni-Stroke IME to “install unknown apps”.\n\nOpen the settings screen, allow it, and try again.

Hold a finger still in the writing zone to switch to voice input. It works out by itself when you have stopped talking and commits the text, so there is nothing to press at the end (touching the screen while it listens does not cut you off). Press ✕ to cancel. The hold is longer than a tap, so tapping for punctuation works as before.

By default only on-device speech recognition is used. Neither the audio nor the recognised text leaves the device. On-device recognition needs Android 13 or later on a device that supports it.

The microphone is only open from the hold until the session ends; the recogniser is then destroyed and the microphone released. Microphone permission is requested the first time you hold.

Voice input is disabled in password fields (even on-device, saying a password out loud is itself a risk).
Use voice input (hold in the writing zone to start)

When the whole thing you said matches one of the phrases below, it is carried out as a command instead of being typed. Said as part of a sentence it is typed normally, so to write the word “delete” itself, say it inside a sentence.

With continuous voice input on, one hold keeps listening until you say “stop listening” or press ✕. You can keep going — speak, it commits, speak again — without using your hands. If nothing is said twice in a row it stops by itself, so the microphone is never left open while you are silent.

Note: starting (the first hold) still needs a hand. Android does not let apps start listening on a spoken cue (a hotword).
Continuous voice input (keeps listening until you say stop)

New line / send … “enter”, “new line”, “send”
Space … “space”
Delete one character … “delete”, “backspace”
Undo the last dictation … “undo”, “scratch that”
Select all … “select all”
Move the cursor … “go left”, “move left”, “go right”, “move right”
Stop voice input … “stop listening”, “stop dictation”

“On-device only” uses nothing but on-device speech recognition (Android 13 or later). Audio never leaves the device. On devices without it, voice input does not work (it never silently switches to sending audio out).

“Automatic” uses on-device recognition when available and otherwise hands the audio to the device's speech recognition service. Depending on that service, audio may be sent to an external server. Where it goes is up to the service, so this keyboard cannot guarantee it.

Either way, voice input cannot be used in password fields. In email, URL and number fields, and in fields where learning is refused such as incognito tabs, only the “Automatic” route to an external service is blocked.
On-device only — audio never leaves the device (default)
Automatic — use the device\'s speech service when on-device is unavailable

For investigating strokes that are not recognised well. When on, each stroke writes its point count, duration, size, recognition score and rejection reason to the Android log.

 adb logcat -s UniStroke

Not needed for normal use (off by default). What you type is never logged.

The dictionary used for English word suggestions is generated from the English word list of the Android Open Source Project\'s keyboard (LatinIME). Words flagged there as possibly offensive are left out, and rare words are dropped to keep the file small.\n\nLatinIME is distributed under the Apache License 2.0. Its copyright notice and the licence follow.

The dictionary used for on-device kana-kanji conversion is generated from the open-source dictionary published by Google\'s Mozc project (the vocabulary, part-of-speech definitions and connection costs of dictionary_oss).\n\nMozc is distributed under the BSD 3-Clause licence, reproduced in full below.

Choosing left-handed moves the button column to the right edge and swaps the zones (digits on the left third, letters on the right two-thirds). On a large unfolded screen the panel is placed on your writing-hand side.

On a large screen you can drag the grip on the panel's top edge to move it. Left and right it snaps to an edge; up and down it snaps into a corner when released near one and otherwise stays where you let go. If the panel hides a URL bar or a send button, just move it up out of the way. The position is kept for next time.

Hold [?] in the writing area to open this screen at any time.
Right-handed (buttons on the left, letters on the left)
Left-handed (buttons on the right, letters on the right)
Sample (● is the start, the arrow is the end)
Write it in the box below, the same way as the sample

Your way of writing these letters has been saved:\n%s
This input method uses a few unusual letter shapes (A, K, X, Y, B and others). Practising just 9 letters lets recognition adapt to the way you write. Start now?

When a stroke is misread and you “erase it with backspace and write it again”, the correction is remembered automatically.

The original stroke is recorded as a candidate for the letter you ended up with, and is promoted to a personal template once the same way of writing appears twice (a single slip is not learned). Before promotion it is checked against the standard shapes of other letters and skipped if it could be confused with one. There are at most 2 personal templates per letter and their bonus at recognition time is tiny (+0.02), so they never override the standard shapes by much.

Note: only “exactly the last stroke was erased” can be tracked — that is, a backspace that removes the letter you just wrote.

Learned letters are listed below (and marked with a dot in the stroke chart). ★ marks shapes saved in Stroke training; they are kept in preference to automatically learned ones.

For the unusual shapes such as A, K, X and Y (K and X are single strokes with a loop; B, D, P and R go up from the lower left before the bumps), practising first in Stroke training above is the surest way.

Shapes saved in training are used as soon as you switch to the keyboard.

Choose the letters to reset. Their learned data (automatically learned strokes and the shapes ★ saved in Stroke training) is deleted, and those letters go back to being recognised by the standard shapes only.
%1$s\n\nThe learned data for these %2$d letters will be deleted. This cannot be undone.
Learned data for the selected letters was deleted

Everything learned about how you write will be deleted. Recognition may get worse.

This deletes the automatically learned personal templates and the shapes (★) saved in Stroke training. Only the standard shapes will be used, so letters where personal habits show, such as A, K, X, Y and B, may be recognised less well.

After resetting, running Stroke training again restores accuracy quickly.
Only the standard shapes are being used now. If recognition feels worse, save your shapes again in Stroke training.
Strokes (each is a single stroke; where it starts matters)

Common (both zones)
 Space … a horizontal line from left to right
 Backspace … a horizontal line from right to left. Right after you pick a suggestion it puts back what you had written
 Return … a diagonal from upper right to lower left. Commits the word in progress and sends Enter; in fields that ask for “Search” or “Send” it runs that action instead
 Up-swipe (a vertical line from bottom to top) … Shift (next letter capital → Caps Lock → off)
 Extended Shift … a diagonal “＼” from upper left to lower right, or “／” from lower left to upper right
 Tap (a dot) … Punctuation Shift
 Hold (press and stay still) … voice input (can be turned off in Settings)

Letter zone (left side)
 A a peak (lower left → top → lower right). The top may be rounded or off-centre
 B up from the lower left, then two clockwise bumps, upper and lower
 C an open counter-clockwise arc from the upper right
 D up from the lower left, then one large clockwise arc
 E the Greek letter ε: from the upper right an upper arc to the left, back at the middle, a lower arc to the left, out to the lower right
 F across the top from right to left, then down
 G the same shape as the digit 6 (down from the upper right to the lower left, closing a counter-clockwise loop at the bottom)
 H a vertical line down, then a hump on the right
 I a vertical line from top to bottom
 J down, then hook up to the left
 K “∝”: enter from the upper right heading down-left, then without making a corner loop clockwise and leave to the lower right, as one continuous curve (the looped form is the official one)
 L down, then right
 M an M zigzag starting at the lower left
 N an N zigzag starting at the lower left (a rounded N also works)
 O a counter-clockwise circle from the top
 P up from the lower left, ending with the upper bump
 Q close a counter-clockwise circle, then flick right across the top
 R up from the lower left, the upper bump, then a diagonal leg to the lower right
 S an S
 T across the top from left to right, then down
 U down from the upper left, round the bottom, up to the upper right
 V “v-”: write a v, then flick the end horizontally to the right (the flick is what tells it from U)
 W a W
 X the mirror image of K: enter from the upper left heading down-right, loop counter-clockwise with no corner and leave to the lower left (the looped form is the official one)
 Y from the valley of a U go up to the upper right, then straight down a long way to the lower left (the original form that makes a loop and leaves to the upper right also works)
 Z a Z

Number zone (right side)
 0–9 use this method's digit shapes. 0 is a circle, 1 a vertical line, 4 a diagonal down to the left and then right, 7 across the top to the right and then down to the left.
Punctuation mode (enter with a tap; ends after one stroke)

After a tap, the next single stroke becomes a symbol. A horizontal line from right to left cancels.

Note: an apostrophe written in the middle of a word stays part of that word (don't). Right after you pick a suggestion, . , ! ? : ; are tucked against the word and followed by a space.
Extended Character mode (enter with “＼”; ends after one stroke)

Write the diagonal “＼” from upper left to lower right (or “／” from lower left to upper right), and the next single stroke becomes a special character. A horizontal line from right to left cancels.

 • tap
 ° a circle
 + “∝”
 − a line left → right
 × a diagonal, upper right → lower left
 ÷ two loops, then to the upper right
 ¡ up (vertical line)
 = a Z
 £ down, then right (L)
 ¿ from the lower right to the left, then up
 ‘ up, then right
 ’ up, then left
 § an S
 ß a B
 © a C (top to bottom)
 ¢ a C (bottom to top)
 € Ɛ (same as E)
 ™ an M
 ® an R
 ¥ in from the upper left to the lower right, a loop at the bottom, out to the upper right

Note: the recogniser first rules out candidates that differ in “the nature of the shape itself”. A stroke that is not straight never becomes a straight-line symbol (I, space, backspace, return, shift, ＼／), and a stroke that doubles back sideways three times (such as E) never becomes F, L, T or C. This is why a tall, narrow E is unlikely to turn into I or F.

Note: for K and X the single stroke with a loop is the official shape. K is a continuous curve that “enters from the upper right heading down-left and, with no corner, loops clockwise and leaves to the lower right” (X is its mirror image, counter-clockwise). The loopless “＜” and “＞” shapes are recognised unreliably, so make the loop as in the sample. The sample is drawn from a formula joining a line, a 270-degree arc and a line by their tangents, so it has no corner, and the training screen plays it back in the order it is written.
Note: the Accent mode (accented letters) of the original method is not implemented.
Note: in the original method X is two strokes, “＼” then “／”. Here “＼” is the Extended Shift, so only the one-stroke X (the mirror image of K) is used.

Switches the whole app between English and Japanese: both what you see and how the keyboard behaves.

 English … letters only. The suggestion bar predicts English words and the top-left button deletes a word
 日本語 (Japanese) … romaji-to-kana input with kana-kanji conversion. The top-left button switches abc ⇄ kana

“Follow system” uses Japanese when the device language is Japanese and English otherwise.
Follow system / 端末の言語に合わせる

The word you are writing is shown underlined, and the suggestion bar offers ways to finish it. Tap a suggestion to enter that word and a space. A space stroke commits exactly what you wrote; nothing is auto-corrected.\n\nIn password, email, URL and number fields no suggestions are shown and each letter is entered directly.
Capitalise the start of sentences automatically

These features are Premium. All of them are available during the trial.

• Voice input and voice commands
• Stroke learning (adapts recognition to the way you write)

Basic typing — strokes and word suggestions — keeps working after the trial ends.

It is a one-time purchase. With the same Google account you can get it back after changing phones or reinstalling, using “Restore purchase”.
